from PIL import Image,ImageOps,ImageDraw

    ims=[]
    for i in range(start,end+1):
        im=Image.open(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02}.png').convert('RGB')
        im.thumbnail((612,810))
        tile=Image.new('RGB',(632,845),'#dddddd')
        tile.paste(im,((632-im.width)//2,25))
        ImageDraw.Draw(tile).text((8,6),f'Page {i}',fill='black')
        ims.append(tile)
    sheet=Image.new('RGB',(632*len(ims),845),'white')

print('Contact sheets saved.')

strengths: The mean-point construction is a useful, original practical contribution to three-view geometry. Adding an approximate centroid correspondence enables four-point hypothesis generation through existing five-point and P3P solvers. This simple construction offers a credible alternative to substantially more complicated dedicated solvers.

The empirical support is extensive: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, evaluations within PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, and supplementary experiments varying noise, scene geometry, outliers and thresholds. The alternative metric including all three camera pairs helps establish that the improvements extend beyond the main evaluation metric.

Benefits remain when the five-point baseline receives comparable improvements. With +R+F+ENM applied to both methods, Table 3 reports PhotoTourism AUC@10 of 76.16 for 4p3v(M) versus 76.20 for 5pt+P3P, with runtimes of 44.51 versus 56.52 ms. Similar savings occur on Cambridge and Aachen. These results support the practical value of the contribution.

The ablations explain the importance of refinement, filtering and early non-minimal refitting. The shift magnitude and refinement iterations are selected using an excluded validation scene. The accessible method description, code/data archive links, named solver implementations and experimental settings provide a substantial basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison against the homotopy baseline has a material caveat. Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports approximately 45 ms for loading its network/data once per RANSAC run. This is substantial relative to the reported 60–67 ms total runtimes and is potentially amortizable across successive estimates. Timings with the baseline already initialized are needed to substantiate the claimed speed advantage over HC.

The strongest speed–accuracy claim is insufficiently tested against the fully enhanced five-point baseline: Figure 4 omits its +R+F variants. Table 3 shows that the most accurate 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM variant improves PhotoTourism AUC@10 from 76.20 to 77.14 over the fully enhanced baseline, while increasing runtime from 56.52 to 112.60 ms. The efficiency claim should be qualified by operating point; uncertainty estimates would also help interpret the smaller accuracy differences.

The theoretical support establishes an image-space error bound proportional to triangle extent, leaving pose conditioning and refinement convergence uncontrolled. Figure 9 demonstrates nonzero errors even with noiseless correspondences, and Table 2 shows substantial dependence on refitting, especially for the affine solver. The assertion that scene dependence becomes negligible after ENM is stronger than the theoretical support and should remain restricted to the tested configurations.

All real-data experiments retain cycle-consistent SuperPoint/LightGlue matches visible in all three views. Consequently, the natural ability of the (5,5,3) baseline to exploit additional two-view-only correspondences is unevaluated. This limits conclusions about comparative performance in reconstruction pipelines with partial visibility.

A localized reporting ambiguity appears in Table 7: the Cambridge rows for 4p3v(M)+R+F and 4p3v(M)+R+F+ENM exactly repeat the corresponding affine-method rows across all reported metrics and runtime. These entries require clarification and reduce confidence in that particular ablation.
